public_rationale: The plain reading is that AI investment was paid for almost entirely with debt. The evidence for 2025 to early 2026 says otherwise. Bank of America found the big hyperscalers could fund near-term capex from cash and borrowed mainly for flexibility. Their 2025 operating cash flow, about $577B, dwarfed the rise in their debt. OpenAI's biggest raise just before the post was a $110B equity round. Debt was growing and important, and Oracle and neoclouds leaned on it heavily. But 'almost entirely by debt' overstates its role across the AI build-out in the period described.
limitations: 'The AI bubble' has no defined scope. A narrower reading (Oracle, neoclouds, SPV-financed data centers) would fit his claim better.
Off-balance-sheet debt may understate how much of the build-out is borrowed.
Private credit funds are debt vehicles by nature, so that part of his sentence is trivially true.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The AI bubble and the private equity and credit funds backing it are fueled almost entirely by debt.

statement.excerpt: And remember: the AI bubble, along with the massive private equity and credit funds backing it, is fueled almost entirely by debt.

from_speaker: along with the massive private equity and credit funds backing it
is fueled almost entirely by debt
our_interpretation: Plain reading: AI investment (mainly data-center and compute spending by hyperscalers and AI labs) was paid for almost entirely with borrowed money, not with operating cash flow or equity.
He named no period. I use the latest period public evidence could describe before the post: calendar 2025 through the post date, 2026-03-10.
Private credit funds are debt providers by nature, so that part is close to true by definition. The test is whether the AI build-out as a whole was almost entirely debt-financed.
criteria.support_condition: Sources show that the large majority of AI capex and AI lab funding in 2025 to early 2026 came from borrowing.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Sources show that most AI capex was funded from operating cash flow, or that major AI funding came as equity.

evidence.excerpt: BofA pointed out that while the companies can fund their near-term capital expenditures with cash, they are tapping debt markets for balance-sheet flexibility and better cost of capital.
evidence.explanation: The biggest AI spenders could fund their capex from cash. Debt was a choice, not the main fuel.

evidence.excerpt: Operating cash flow for the big five hyperscalers is expected to hit $577 billion this year from $378 billion in 2023, while debt should climb from $356 billion to $433 billion.
evidence.explanation: 2025 operating cash flow of about $577B is far bigger than the roughly $77B rise in debt. That points to cash, not debt, as the main funding source.

evidence.excerpt: OpenAI said on Friday it is raising $110 billion in a blockbuster funding round that would value the ChatGPT maker at $840 billion
evidence.explanation: The largest AI lab's biggest raise, just before the post, was an equity round valued on OpenAI's shares, not debt.

evidence.excerpt: Unlike the other AI hyperscalers, it will have negative free cash flow until 2029, meaning its capex will exceed cash from operations
evidence.explanation: Oracle is the exception that relies on outside financing. This partly backs his view for some players, but not for the industry as a whole.
